clinical_category: Osteoporosis - recognition of fragility fracture and impaired bone strength
blueprint_topic: Pathophysiology and manifestations of reduced bone strength
stem: A 72-year-old client fractures the wrist after falling from standing height. Which interpretation by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.A: A low-trauma fracture can be a sign of osteoporosis because reduced bone mass or altered bone structure decreases bone strength and increases fracture susceptibility; bone-health evaluation is warranted.
options.B: A fracture from standing height rules out osteoporosis because osteoporotic fractures occur only after high-energy trauma.
options.C: Osteoporosis primarily affects skin and soft tissue, so it would not explain increased skeletal fragility after a minor fall.
options.D: If the client had no bone pain before the fall, osteoporosis can be excluded because osteoporosis is usually painful before a fracture occurs.

rationale: A is correct. Current NIAMS guidance defines osteoporosis as a bone disease in which bone mineral density and bone mass decrease or bone quality/structure changes, reducing bone strength and increasing fracture risk. Osteoporosis is often silent until a fracture occurs, and affected bones may fracture after minor trauma such as a fall from standing height that would not normally break healthy bone. Therefore, this low-trauma wrist fracture should prompt consideration of osteoporosis and appropriate bone-health evaluation rather than being dismissed as ordinary trauma. B is incorrect because minor falls are a recognized mechanism of osteoporotic fragility fractures. C is incorrect because osteoporosis is a skeletal disease. D is incorrect because osteoporosis commonly causes no symptoms before fracture. The final item converts the source's definition recall into clinical recognition of the pathophysiologic consequence of impaired bone strength without requiring an unnecessary DXA threshold.
educational_objective: Recognize a fracture after minimal trauma in an older adult as a possible manifestation of osteoporosis caused by reduced bone strength and understand that osteoporosis may be clinically silent before fracture.
source_organization: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases (NIAMS), National Institutes of Health
source_document_title: Osteoporosis; Bone Mineral Density Tests: What the Numbers Mean; Preventing Another Broken Bone
source_locator: NIAMS 'Osteoporosis' → Overview: osteoporosis develops when bone mineral density/bone mass decreases or bone structure/strength changes, causing decreased bone strength and increased fracture risk; osteoporosis is often silent until fracture and fragile bones may break after minor trauma. NIAMS 'Bone Mineral Density Tests' → BMD testing helps identify osteoporosis and assess fracture risk. NIAMS 'Preventing Another Broken Bone' → a fracture in an older adult may be a sign of osteoporosis and should prompt bone-health evaluation.
source_claim_supported: Current NIAMS sources directly support reduced bone mass/quality and decreased bone strength as the basis of osteoporosis, low-trauma fracture susceptibility, the silent nature of disease before fracture, and follow-up evaluation after an older adult sustains a fragility-type fracture.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity → Physiological Adaptation: recognize and manage acute, chronic or life-threatening physical health conditions; apply pathophysiology and identify manifestations or complications of altered body-system function.
correction_summary: Fresh re-audit of the source's low-level osteoporosis definition into an applied fragility-fracture recognition item. The final version uses authoritative NIH/NIAMS evidence, tests the consequence of reduced bone strength after minimal trauma, preserves the silent-disease concept, and avoids unsupported or unnecessary DXA cutoffs.
audit_findings: The source concept was correct but tested only a definition with weak distractors.
Fresh NIAMS review directly supports low bone mass/quality, reduced strength and fractures after minor falls such as standing-height falls.
NIAMS also confirms osteoporosis is frequently silent until a fracture occurs, preventing absence of prior pain from being used as an exclusion criterion.
Distractors test high-trauma-only misconception, incorrect tissue target and symptom-before-fracture misconception; none is defensible.
